newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler unveils "driverless" vehicle test area.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler unveils "driverless" vehicle test area.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. said Tuesday it expected to take four weeks out of its vehicle development cycle with what it described as the country's first "driverless" vehicle test facility.

Called the Automated Durability Road (ADR), the system uses three robot-driven vehicles to maneuver around a 1.3-mile oval track, covering ground intended to replicate rough road conditions -- severe potholes, bumpy railroad track crossings and cobblestone surfaces.
"This is the only track of its type in the United States," said Sue Cischke, general manager for scientific laboratories and proving grounds.

Chrysler said the primary reason it developed the ADR was to accelerate its product development and improve 'real-world' test data from the first phase of conventional durability testing, which typically takes six to eight weeks.
Under the ADR's durability tests, Chrysler said it takes 2,500 miles on the track to equal the effect of a vehicle driving 100,000 miles.

Because humans can only drive about four hours a day on severe road conditions, Chrysler said it decided to use robots, who can drive day and night, and not be tempted to let up on the accelerator or swerve to avoid large potholes.
"We think we can take the testing time down from six weeks to less than two weeks and that's a huge advantage in our ever shrinking product cycle time," Cischke said.
The system is located at Chrysler's Proving Grounds in Chelsea, Mich. The ADR uses two sensors at the front of the vehicle to pick up frequencies from a guide wire imbedded in the track.

That information is relayed to a computer placed in the passenger seat, which controls the speed and steering of the vehicle. Levers on the robot act as feet and hands, pushing on the brake and accelerator and shifting gears.
Vehicles typically travel between 25-30 mph and have reached top speeds of 45 mph.

Chrysler said it did not foresee public applications of the technology, however, because of the safety systems needed to prevent accidents. Also, Chrysler said equipping the vehicles costs about $50,000 each.
